summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.
tangentialFactors:
Mayotte's position is unusual in its region: it is one of very few places in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where same-sex marriage can be performed, a consequence of the 1975 vote to remain part of France rather than of any local legislative initiative.

The gap between statutory protection and daily experience is the recurring pattern in reporting from the island. Couples and trans residents hold the full French suite of rights, yet the 2023 account of a marriage at Sada town hall describes a long and complicated process shaped by the social environment of a predominantly Muslim island.

The failures documented by the CGLPL are systemic rather than local to any one prison: the watchdog's opinion covers all French places of deprivation of liberty, so a trans detainee held on Mayotte is subject to the same documented risks as one held in mainland establishments.
localsOnly:
Residents subject to French criminal procedure are placed in custody according to the gender marker on their identity document, not according to anatomy. For trans women this means routine placement in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them.

The CGLPL's opinion of 25 May 2021 draws on referrals it has received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people, and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. The violations it describes as persisting are treated as binding standards and known failures for French establishments, including those on Mayotte.

Legal gender change has been simplified by a vote of the National Assembly, and the simplified civil-status procedure is available on the island as French law applies to the department.

Anyone on the island seeking a lawyer experienced with LGBT clients will find no referenced practitioner in the local directory entries for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and the other listed towns. The directory points instead to a Paris-based lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation whose practice covers persons and family law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mayotte-specific inspection by the CGLPL is sourced here. The four establishments named in its 2021 opinion are mainland prisons, so the extension to Mayotte rests on the opinion covering all French places of deprivation of liberty rather than on a site visit to the island.

The inventory contains no data on how gender-marker changes are processed locally, on waiting times or refusals at the Mayotte civil status office, or on any challenge brought on the island.

No sourced evidence covers hate-crime prosecution, discrimination complaints or police conduct toward trans people in Mayotte specifically. The 2023 reporting on the Sada town hall marriage documents social obstruction rather than a legal or enforcement action.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, and the availability of competent interpretation or culturally competent care on the island, are not addressed by any source in this inventory.
